Summary  
The paper introduces “Scientific Regret Minimization” (SRM), an iterative process that uses a high-capacity neural network to reveal where simple psychological choice models of moral judgement are missing features, then adds human-interpretable “axes of moral difference” (e.g. age, fitness, status) until the refined model matches the neural network’s predictive accuracy.  Preregistered MTurk experiments confirm three newly discovered moral principles (criminal de-humanisation, age of responsibility, asymmetric responsibility).  The methodology is offered as a way to build transparent, value-aligned decision rules for autonomous vehicles (AVs) while avoiding spurious correlations that plague black-box systems.  

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[87]  
The extraction follows the mandatory success criteria and verification checklist.  Remaining uncertainty stems from moderate inference when mapping general SRM methodological claims to specific AI-safety-relevant interventions.  

Instruction-set improvement:  the prompt could clarify how to label methodological “framework” papers that do not present ready-made safety interventions, perhaps by giving an explicit rule-of-thumb for inferring interventions from methodological contributions.  

Inference strategy justification  
Interventions (e.g. “apply SRM during model design”) are not explicitly labelled as such in the text; they are moderately inferred from the authors’ stated goals and demonstrations (edge confidence 2–3).  All other nodes strictly follow empirical findings or described mechanisms.  

Extraction completeness explanation  
All causal paths from the three top-level risks (misalignment, dehumanisation bias, spurious feature reliance) through mechanisms, insights, design rationales, implementations, validation evidence and finally to four actionable interventions are covered.  Nodes are de-duplicated and connected; no isolated nodes remain.  

Key limitations  
1. The source focuses on human moral-psychology research; mapping to AV safety interventions requires inference.  
2. Quantitative details (exact statistics) are summarised, not exhaustively encoded, to keep node granularity tractable.  
3. Edge confidence is qualitative; downstream users should verify numeric robustness as needed.
